passage: Many successful people say that the morning is the most important part of the day. They wake up early and follow a routine. A routine is a set of actions you do every day in the same order.
For example, some people wake up, drink water, and then do some exercise. Others prefer to sit quietly and think before they start their day. These habits help people feel ready and calm.
A good routine does not have to be long or complicated. It just needs to be consistent. When you do the same things every morning, your body and mind learn to prepare for the day ahead.
Try to notice your own morning habits. Are they helping you? If not, you can change them slowly, one small step at a time.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A set of actions you do regularly in the same order
Something you do regularly, often without thinking
Always the same; not changing
To get ready for something
vocabulary.example: I prepare my bag the night before.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To like one thing more than another
Physical activity to keep your body healthy
To see or become aware of something
Difficult to understand or do
Achieving what you wanted to achieve
To become or make something better
Peaceful; not worried or excited
vocabulary.example: Take a deep breath and stay calm.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To do something according to a plan or example
At a low speed; not quickly
In the future; forward in time
The way things are arranged in a sequence
vocabulary.example: Do things in the right order.

speaking_prompts: Describe your own morning routine. What do you do first? What do you do last?
What habit would you like to improve or start? Why?
Do you prefer to prepare things the night before or in the morning? Explain.
Talk about a routine that helps you feel calm or ready for the day.

grammar_focus.title: Simple present for habits and routines
grammar_focus.explanation: We use the simple present tense to talk about things we do regularly. Look at these examples from the passage: 'They wake up early', 'Others prefer to sit quietly'. Notice the verb has no change for I/you/we/they, but adds -s for he/she/it.
examples: I wake up at 7am every day.
She follows a strict routine.
We exercise in the morning.
He prefers to work quietly.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences about your own daily habits using the simple present tense.

passage: A good friend is someone you can trust. Trust means that you believe a person will be honest with you and keep your secrets. Without trust, a friendship is not strong.
Good friends also listen to each other. When you have a problem, a real friend does not only give advice. They listen carefully and try to understand how you feel. This is called empathy.
Friendship also needs time. You cannot build a close friendship in one day. It grows slowly through shared experiences, things you do together, like eating, laughing, or helping each other.

Not all friends need to be the same as you. In fact, friends who are different from you can teach you new things and help you see the world in a new way. A good friendship makes both people feel better about life.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The belief that someone is honest and reliable
Telling the truth; not lying
Information that you do not share with others
To pay attention to what someone is saying
Suggestions about what someone should do
The ability to understand how someone else feels
Done or used by two or more people together
Something that happens to you that affects you
Having a strong, warm relationship
To create something over time
To develop and become bigger or stronger
Genuine; not fake or pretend
Not the same as something else
To help someone learn something
vocabulary.example: Friends can teach you a lot.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Two people or things together
vocabulary.example: Both of us enjoyed the trip.

speaking_prompts: Describe a good friend. What makes them special to you?
Talk about a shared experience that made a friendship closer.
What is more important in a friend, honesty or empathy? Why?
Have you ever had a friend who was very different from you? What did you learn from them?

grammar_focus.title: Can for ability and possibility
grammar_focus.explanation: In the passage, we see 'you can trust', 'you cannot build', 'friends can teach'. We use 'can' to talk about ability (what someone is able to do) or possibility. The negative form is 'cannot' or 'can't'.
examples: A good friend can keep secrets.
You can't build trust quickly.
Friends can teach you new things.
I can listen for hours.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences using 'can' or 'can't' about friendship or daily life.

passage: What we eat has a big effect on how we feel. When we eat healthy food, our bodies have more energy and our minds feel clearer. But eating well does not mean you have to follow a complicated diet.

The most important thing is balance. Try to eat a variety of foods, vegetables, fruit, protein, and whole grains. Avoid eating too much sugar or fast food. These foods might taste good, but they do not give your body what it needs.
Water is also very important. Many people forget to drink enough water during the day. When your body does not have enough water, you can feel tired or find it hard to concentrate.
You do not need to change everything at once. Start with small changes. Add one more vegetable to your meals. Drink one more glass of water. Small steps can lead to big results over time.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A result or change caused by something
vocabulary.example: Sleep has a big effect on your mood.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The strength to be active and do things
Having the right amount of different things
Many different types of something
A nutrient in food that helps build your body
vocabulary.example: Eggs are a good source of protein.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To stay away from something on purpose
To focus your attention on something
vocabulary.example: It's hard to concentrate when tired.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The outcome or effect of an action
The food you regularly eat
Occasions when you eat food
vocabulary.example: I have three meals a day.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To cause something to happen
vocabulary.example: Bad habits can lead to problems.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To not remember to do something
Complete; not processed or refined
To put something extra into something
vocabulary.example: Add more vegetables to your diet.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: As much as is needed

speaking_prompts: Describe your typical diet. Is it balanced? What could you improve?
What food habits do you find hard to change? Why?
How does what you eat affect how you feel during the day?

grammar_focus.title: Imperatives for advice and instructions
grammar_focus.explanation: The passage uses imperative sentences to give advice: 'Try to eat a variety', 'Avoid eating too much sugar', 'Start with small changes'. Imperatives use the base form of the verb with no subject. Use 'Don't' for negative imperatives.
examples: Drink more water every day.
Avoid processed food.
Add vegetables to every meal.
Don't forget to sleep well.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 4 pieces of advice for a friend who wants to eat more healthily. Use imperatives.

passage: A goal is something you want to achieve in the future. Without a goal, it is easy to feel lost or unsure about what to do next. Goals give us direction and motivation.

The best goals are specific. Instead of saying 'I want to improve my English', say 'I want to learn 10 new words every week'. A specific goal is easier to measure, you can see if you are making progress or not.
It is also important to be realistic. A goal that is too difficult will make you feel discouraged. Start with something achievable, and then make your goals bigger as you improve.
When you reach a goal, celebrate it, even if it is small. Celebrating progress helps you stay motivated and reminds you that you are moving in the right direction. Then set a new goal and keep going.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To successfully reach a goal after effort
The path or purpose you are moving towards
The reason or desire to do something
Clear and detailed; not general
To find out the size or amount of something
Moving forward; improvement over time
Reasonable and possible to achieve
Feeling less confident or motivated after difficulty
Possible to do; within your ability
To do something enjoyable to mark a success
To help someone remember something
To arrive at or accomplish something
vocabulary.example: I want to reach my target.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To get better at something
Unsure of where to go or what to do
To continue doing something

speaking_prompts: What is a goal you have right now? Is it specific and realistic?
Talk about a goal you have already achieved. How did it feel?
How do you stay motivated when progress is slow?
What is the difference between a dream and a realistic goal?

grammar_focus.title: Want to / Would like to for goals and wishes
grammar_focus.explanation: We use 'want to' and 'would like to' to talk about our goals and desires. 'Want to' is more direct. 'Would like to' is more polite and formal. Both are followed by the infinitive (base verb).
examples: I want to improve my English.
I would like to work abroad.
She wants to achieve her goals.
They would like to travel more.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences about your personal or professional goals using 'want to' or 'would like to'.

passage: People travel for many different reasons. Some travel for fun and relaxation. Others travel to learn about different cultures or to visit family. Some people travel for work.

When you visit a new place, you experience things that are different from your normal life. You might try new food, hear a new language, or see beautiful buildings and nature. These experiences can change the way you think about the world.

Travel can also be challenging. You might get lost, miss your flight, or not understand the local language. But these challenges are also part of the experience. They teach you to be flexible and to solve problems.

You do not always need to travel far to benefit from these experiences. Even visiting a new part of your own city can feel like an adventure. The important thing is to stay curious and open to new things.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The state of being free from stress and worry
The customs, beliefs, and arts of a group of people
vocabulary.example: I love learning about other cultures.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To feel or live through something
vocabulary.example: Travel lets you experience new things.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Usual; what typically happens
vocabulary.example: This is not my normal routine.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Difficult in a way that requires effort
Able to change and adapt easily
vocabulary.example: You need to be flexible when travelling.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To find an answer to a problem
vocabulary.example: How do you solve this problem?

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To gain something useful or helpful
An exciting or unusual experience
Wanting to learn or know more about something
Relating to the area where you are
To fail to catch or be at something
The natural world; plants, animals, land
vocabulary.example: I love spending time in nature.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Willing to accept new ideas or experiences

speaking_prompts: Describe a place you have visited. What did you experience there?

grammar_focus.title: Past simple for completed experiences
grammar_focus.explanation: We use the past simple to talk about completed experiences. Regular verbs add -ed: 'visited', 'tried', 'learned'. Irregular verbs change form: 'went', 'saw', 'heard'. Look for the time markers: 'last year', 'yesterday', 'in 2020'.
examples: I visited a new city last summer.
She tried local food and loved it.
We saw beautiful mountains.
They went to three countries in one week.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about a place you visited or a new experience you had. Use the past simple.

passage: Emotions are a natural part of life. We all feel happy, sad, angry, nervous, or excited at different times. Understanding your emotions can help you manage them better.

Sometimes we feel an emotion without knowing why. This is normal. Emotions can be connected to things that happened in the past or to worries about the future. When you feel a strong emotion, try to stop and ask yourself: what is causing this feeling?

It is important not to hide your emotions all the time. Sharing how you feel with someone you trust can help you feel lighter. Talking about your emotions also helps other people understand you better.

At the same time, try not to react too quickly when you feel a strong emotion like anger. Give yourself time to calm down before you speak or act. This can prevent many problems in your relationships.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A feeling such as happiness, sadness, or anger
To deal with something in a controlled way
Linked or related to something else
vocabulary.example: Stress is connected to poor sleep.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A feeling of anxiety about something that might happen
vocabulary.example: Don't worry about things you can't control.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Powerful and intense
vocabulary.example: She felt a strong sense of pride.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To keep something secret; not show it
To tell or give something to others
vocabulary.example: Share your feelings with a friend.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To believe someone is reliable and honest
To respond to something that happens
vocabulary.example: Try not to react too quickly.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To stop something bad from happening
To make something happen
To become or make less anxious or upset
vocabulary.example: Take time to calm down first.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A connection between two or more people
Normal; existing without being forced
Feeling less burdened or worried

speaking_prompts: How do you manage strong emotions like anger or anxiety?
Do you find it easy or difficult to share your feelings? Why?
Talk about a time when you reacted too quickly to something. What happened?
What emotion do you find hardest to manage? How do you deal with it?

grammar_focus.title: When / Before / After, time clauses
grammar_focus.explanation: The passage uses time clauses: 'When you feel a strong emotion, try to stop', 'before you speak or act'. These clauses tell us the timing of actions. The time clause can come first or second in the sentence.
examples: When I feel nervous, I take deep breaths.
Before you react, give yourself a moment.
After she calmed down, she spoke clearly.
I feel better when I share my feelings.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences about your own emotions using 'when', 'before', or 'after'.

passage: People learn in different ways. Some people learn best by reading. Others prefer to listen or to watch. And some people learn by doing, by practising something until they understand it.
Knowing how you learn best is very useful. It can help you study more effectively and feel less frustrated when something is difficult to understand.

One thing that all learners have in common is the need for repetition. When you see or hear something many times, your brain begins to remember it. This is why reviewing new information is so important.

Mistakes are also a key part of learning. When you make a mistake, your brain works hard to understand what went wrong. This process actually helps you remember more. So instead of feeling embarrassed about mistakes, try to see them as opportunities to grow.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To like one option more than another
To do something repeatedly to improve
In a way that produces good results
Feeling upset because you cannot do something
vocabulary.example: I feel frustrated when I make mistakes.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The act of doing or saying something many times
To look at something again to remember or check it
Something done incorrectly
A series of steps that lead to a result
Feeling uncomfortable because of a mistake
A chance to do or achieve something
Shared by many people; happening often
The organ in your head that controls thinking
To keep information in your mind
Not easy; requiring effort
vocabulary.example: Grammar can be difficult at first.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To develop and improve over time

speaking_prompts: How do you learn best, by reading, listening, or doing? Give examples.
Talk about a time you learned something from a mistake.
How do you review new information to help yourself remember it?
Do you feel embarrassed when you make mistakes in English? How do you deal with that?

grammar_focus.title: By + -ing to explain how
grammar_focus.explanation: We use 'by + -ing' to explain the method or way of doing something. In the passage: 'learn by doing', 'by practising something'. The -ing form comes directly after 'by'.
examples: She improved by practising every day.
I learn by making flashcards.
He got better by reading more.
You can grow by accepting mistakes.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences about how you do something, using 'by + -ing'.

passage: Money is something most people think about every day. We earn it, spend it, and sometimes worry about not having enough. Learning to manage money well is one of the most useful skills you can have.
One simple way to manage money is to make a budget. A budget is a plan for how you will spend your money. It helps you see where your money goes and decide what is necessary and what is not.
Many people spend money on things they do not really need. This is sometimes called impulsive spending, buying something because you want it right now, not because it is useful or important.

A good habit is to wait 24 hours before buying something you want but do not need. Often, after a day, the feeling passes and you realise you do not actually want it. This small trick can save you a lot of money over time.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To receive money in exchange for work
A plan for how to spend money
Something you must have or do
Done quickly without thinking carefully
To become aware of something; to understand
vocabulary.example: I realised I didn't need it.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To keep money rather than spending it
vocabulary.example: Try to save 10% of your income.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Helpful and practical
vocabulary.example: This is a very useful skill.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A clever way of doing something
Goes away or ends (of a feeling or time)
To choose one option after thinking
vocabulary.example: Decide what is important to you.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: An organised set of ideas to achieve something
vocabulary.example: Have a plan for your money.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To use money to pay for things
vocabulary.example: Don't spend more than you earn.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: In reality; in fact
Easy to understand or do
Gradually, during a long period
vocabulary.example: Small savings add up over time.

speaking_prompts: Do you have a budget? How do you manage your money?
Talk about something you bought impulsively. Did you regret it?
What is the difference between something necessary and something you just want?
What is a simple money habit that you think is useful?

grammar_focus.title: Comparative adjectives
grammar_focus.explanation: We compare things using comparative adjectives. Short adjectives add -er: simple -> simpler. Long adjectives use 'more': impulsive -> more impulsive. Always use 'than' when comparing two things.
examples: A budget is simpler than you think.
This option is more useful than the other.
She is more careful with money now.
Saving is easier when you have a plan.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences comparing two things related to money, habits, or daily life. Use comparative adjectives.

passage: Green spaces are areas of nature in or near cities, like parks, gardens, or forests. Research shows that spending time in green spaces is good for both your physical and mental health.

When people spend time in nature, their stress levels often decrease. The fresh air, the sounds of birds, and the sight of trees and plants help the mind relax. Some scientists believe that we have a natural connection to nature that goes back thousands of years.
Green spaces are also important for communities. They give people a place to exercise, meet others, and relax outside. Children who grow up near green spaces tend to be more active and creative.

Unfortunately, in many cities, green spaces are disappearing as more buildings are constructed. This is why it is important to protect and create more green areas, not just for nature, but for the wellbeing of the people who live there.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Careful study to find new information
Relating to the body
Relating to the mind
vocabulary.example: Take care of your mental health.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To become smaller or less
A link or relationship between things
vocabulary.example: There is a connection between sleep and mood.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A group of people living in the same area
To usually do or be something
Good at thinking of new ideas
Sadly; used when something is bad
Going away or becoming less visible
To build something
To keep something safe from harm
A state of being happy, healthy, and comfortable
Moving and doing physical activities
A part of a place or region

speaking_prompts: How often do you spend time in nature or green spaces? How does it make you feel?
Do you think cities should have more green spaces? Why or why not?
Talk about a place in nature that is special to you.

grammar_focus.title: Present continuous for ongoing changes
grammar_focus.explanation: We use the present continuous (am/is/are+-ing) to describe things that are changing or happening right now or around now. In the passage: 'green spaces are disappearing'. This shows an ongoing trend.
examples: Green spaces are disappearing in many cities.
The climate is changing quickly.
More people are moving to cities.
Technology is improving every year.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 sentences about changes happening in the world or your life right now. Use the present continuous.

passage: We all have the same 24 hours in a day. But some people seem to do much more with their time than others. What is their secret?

The answer is often about priorities. A priority is something that is more important than other things. When you know your priorities, you spend your time on things that matter, not on things that are just urgent but not important.
Many people spend a lot of time on things that feel busy but do not help them reach their goals. Checking your phone constantly or watching too much television are common examples.

One useful approach is to decide the three most important things you need to do each day and focus on those first. This is sometimes called the 'three big tasks' method. When you finish those, everything else feels easier. Try it for one week and notice the difference it makes.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: Something more important than other things
To be important or significant
Needing immediate attention
vocabulary.example: This is urgent, do it now.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: All the time; without stopping
A way of dealing with something
To give your full attention to something
vocabulary.example: Focus on one task at a time.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A particular way of doing something
A change or contrast between two things
To appear to be a certain way
Something you want to achieve
Practical and helpful
Happening often or found in many places
vocabulary.example: This is a very common problem.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To complete something
vocabulary.example: Finish the most important task first.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: To arrive at or achieve something
vocabulary.example: How will you reach your goals?

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: The key reason behind a success
vocabulary.example: What is the secret to success?

speaking_prompts: What are your top three priorities in life right now? Why?
What activities waste your time the most? How could you change this?
Do you have a method for managing your time? Does it work?
What is the difference between something urgent and something important?

grammar_focus.title: Comparative: more than / less than
grammar_focus.explanation: We use 'more than' and 'less than' to compare things. Multi-syllable adjectives always use 'more' or 'less': 'more important than', 'less urgent than'. This is different from short adjective comparatives (-er).
examples: Rest is more important than staying busy.
Email is less urgent than you think.
This method is more effective than the old one.
Sleep matters more than most people realise.
grammar_focus.practice_task: Write 3 comparisons about how you use your time. Use 'more than' or 'less than'.
